nameStory: The 'wild raisin' name comes from this shrub's small, dark berries that wrinkle up like raisins when they dry out on the branches. Indigenous peoples and early settlers discovered these sweet-tart fruits made a decent snack when other food was scarce, though they're nowhere near as tasty as actual grapes!
description: Northern wild raisin is a medium-sized deciduous shrub that typically grows 6-12 feet tall with an upright, somewhat rounded shape. It's a member of the viburnum family, sporting clusters of small white flowers in late spring followed by berries that change from green to pink to blue-black as they ripen. The oval leaves have a leathery feel and turn beautiful shades of orange and red in fall, making this an attractive native shrub for both wildlife and people to enjoy.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves with smooth or very slightly toothed edges, arranged in opposite pairs along the stems. Feel the leaves - they have a distinctly thick, leathery texture that's quite different from most other shrubs.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers about 3-5 inches across bloom in late May to early June. Each individual flower is small but together they create showy, creamy-white displays that smell faintly sweet.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Berries start green, turn pink or red, then ripen to blue-black in late summer. They're about the size of a pea and often you'll see different colors on the same cluster as they ripen at different rates.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms an upright shrub 6-12 feet tall with multiple stems from the base. The branching pattern is fairly regular and symmetrical, giving it a neat, tidy appearance even in the wild.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth gray bark on younger stems, developing shallow grooves on older, thicker branches. The bark has a slightly rough texture when you run your fingers over it.

habitat: Look for northern wild raisin in wetland edges, swamps, and moist woodlands throughout New England. It thrives in acidic soils and partial shade, often growing alongside other moisture-loving natives like red maple, winterberry, and sweet pepperbush. You'll frequently spot it in that transition zone between open wetlands and drier upland forests.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green in May, followed by the showy white flower clusters in late May to early June that attract various pollinators including bees and butterflies.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and small green berries begin forming. The thick, leathery leaves remain dark green and provide good identification clues throughout the hot months.
seasonality.fall: Berries ripen through shades of pink and red to final blue-black, while leaves turn brilliant orange, red, or purple. This is when the shrub is most spectacular and easiest to spot.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the smooth gray bark and opposite branching pattern. Some dried berries may persist, and the sturdy upright form remains recognizable.

funFact: The berries of northern wild raisin change color so gradually that a single cluster can look like a tiny box of mixed jellybeans, with green, pink, red, and blue-black berries all hanging together at the same time!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its close cousin southern wild raisin (Viburnum nudum), but northern wild raisin has much thicker, more leathery leaves. Memory trick: 'Northern needs thick leaves for harsh weather' - if you can easily bend the leaf, it's probably the southern species.
contextualKnowledge: Some botanists consider northern wild raisin to be just a variety of southern wild raisin rather than a separate species, which is why you might see it listed as 'Viburnum nudum var. cassinoides' in some field guides. Don't let the scientific name confusion worry you - the thick, leathery leaves are your reliable field mark!
compareHints: Among New England viburnums, northern wild raisin's thick, leathery leaves with smooth edges make it distinctive. Nannyberry has similar smooth-edged leaves but they're much thinner and more flexible. The arrowwoods have distinctly toothed leaves, while hobblebush has much larger, heart-shaped leaves with prominent veins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's viburnums, hobblebush is easily distinguished by its large heart-shaped leaves and drooping, rooting branches - most other viburnums grow more upright.
Among New England's viburnums, mapleleaf viburnum is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves - all other viburnums have simple oval or toothed leaves.
Unlike other viburnums in New England, guelder-rose is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves.
Among New England's viburnums, nannyberry stands out for its tree-like size and glossy leaves with fine teeth all around the edges.
Unlike hobblebush with its large heart-shaped leaves or mapleleaf viburnum with maple-like foliage, southern arrowwood has distinctly toothed, oval leaves with straight parallel veins.
Among the viburnums, northern arrowwood is distinguished by its combination of coarsely toothed leaves, smooth leaf surfaces, and preference for wet areas.

Unlike our native viburnums, Japanese snowball produces those distinctive perfectly round, sterile flower clusters rather than the flat-topped fertile flower clusters of species like nannyberry or arrowwood.

Among New England's viburnums, linden viburnum is most easily distinguished by its heart-shaped leaves - most other viburnums have either lobed leaves (like mapleleaf viburnum), elongated leaves (like nannyberry), or toothed oval leaves (like the arrowwoods).
Wright viburnum differs from native viburnums like arrowwoods and wild raisins by its more pronounced leaf venation and the distinctive red-to-black berry color change.
Siebold's viburnum stands out from other viburnums by its distinctively large, deeply ribbed leaves with parallel veining - most other viburnums have smaller leaves or different vein patterns.
Among New England's viburnums, squashberry is unique for its three-lobed, maple-like leaves - most other viburnums have either simple oval leaves (like nannyberry) or more complex tooth patterns.
Among the arrowwoods, downy arrowwood is distinguished by its fuzzy leaf undersides and earlier bloom time compared to southern arrowwood, which has broader leaves and longer leaf stems.
Among New England's viburnums, blackhaw stands out for its particularly hard wood and oval berries - most other viburnums have round berries.

**[UNCERTAIN]** Unlike the more common mapleleaf viburnum with its maple-shaped leaves or the arrowwoods with their toothed oval leaves, veiny viburnum's leaves are distinguished primarily by their extraordinarily prominent venation rather than their overall shape.

Tea viburnum differs from other New England viburnums by its oval berries that turn from red to black, rather than the round berries that stay red, blue, or black found in species like guelder-rose or arrowwoods.
Unlike native New England viburnums such as hobblebush or arrowwoods, wayfaring-tree has distinctly wrinkled, velvety leaves rather than smooth ones.
Among New England viburnums, Korean spice viburnum stands out for its incredible fragrance and compact size.
Among the viburnums, southern wild raisin stands out for its completely smooth leaf edges - most other viburnums have toothed leaves.
Unlike native New England viburnums which are all deciduous, leatherleaf viburnum keeps its leaves year-round.
